made.p: A curriculum outline for trainers, a toolkit of training methods, learning mechanics and session recipes, and a report on AI skills and training. Gaps were filled by research.

The source material was reviewed and fact-checked on 17 November 2026. Figures that held up are listed under Training today in numbers, each with its source. Claims that did not hold up were corrected or removed, including some in our own sources.

147 of the 149 topics have had their sources opened and carry an evidence rating. Two have not, and say so. Papers were read in summary, not in full, and some were read on a university or index copy because the publisher page would not open.
Every practice carries a rating from A to E, shown as a letter, five bars and a word. Colour is never used for evidence: colour means the stage of the Playbook.
Planned, designed and built with an AI assistant, with a person signing off each step: the content review, the site plan, the design, then the build.

items: Second source check. 147 of 149 topics now have sources opened, linked and rated. Topics 1.20 and 4.12 are still to check.
Stage 1 re-checked in full. Ratings lowered for sleep, learning styles, stress, the early win and mindset.
All 15 myths and all 18 findings on Home now have an opened source. Three myth verdicts changed.
Reading list: 19 of 22 items confirmed and linked. The five World Economic Forum figures re-confirmed on the report page.
Google Workspace and Notion topics checked against the product help pages.
Still to do: topics 1.20 and 4.12, eleven mistakes on Home, three reading-list items, and swapping copies of papers for the journal pages.
Source check of Stages 2 to 9 started. 66 topics in those stages now have sources opened, linked and rated. The check stopped when the search allowance for the session ran out, so it is not finished.
Text corrected where a source said something different, and unsupported figures removed or softened across all nine stages.
An illustrative example added to every topic.
Twelve case studies written from public sources. Seven have independent evidence of results. Five are marked as thin evidence.
Four myths, three findings and three mistakes on Home checked against their sources. Eight glossary definitions corrected.
Still to do then: finish the source check for the remaining topics, the reading list, the other eleven myths, and the Google Workspace and Notion topics.
Content reviewed and fact-checked.
Site plan and design system agreed.
Home, Playbook landing and Stage page designs signed off.
First build in React: Home, Playbook, eight stage pages.
Toolkit, Evidence, Case studies, About and Search pages built as first versions for review.
Gap review: a ninth stage and 59 topics added to the Playbook.
Stage 1's 17 original topics written as drafts from the curriculum outline.
24 of the 47 references in those drafts checked against their published summaries. Six passages corrected where the source said something different.
Recall questions and related-topic links added to the written topics.
All 149 Playbook topics now have a draft. 89 are written from the curriculum outline and 60 from general knowledge. Each says which.
27 references are checked against their published summaries. The rest are marked not checked.
The 11 remaining myths, a glossary, template outlines and a reading list added as drafts.
Still to do then: the case studies, evidence ratings for Stages 2 to 9, and source checks for Stages 2 to 9.

glossary.def: Objectives, activities and assessment all point at the same target.
Judging someone by a task close to the real one.
A programme that mixes face-to-face and online learning on purpose. It often combines live and self-paced parts.
A group of related details that the mind handles as one thing.
The mental effort a task demands of working memory.
A group who share a field, interact regularly and learn from each other how to do it better.
A list of the knowledge, skills and behaviours that make someone capable in a role.
The settling of a memory over time, much of it during sleep.
Practice aimed at one weakness, at the edge of ability, with feedback.
A challenge during learning, such as spacing or self-testing, that slows progress at first and makes learning last longer.
The responsibility to take reasonable steps to keep participants safe from foreseeable harm.
How big a difference is, as opposed to whether it is statistically significant.
Support that helps a beginner gets in the way of an expert.
Drawing learning out of a group, as opposed to presenting to it.
A check during learning that is used to adjust what happens next.
Producing an answer before being given it.
Mixing related kinds of task in practice.
A checklist or reference used at the moment of need.
A named process by which learning happens, such as spacing or feedback.
A study that combines the results of many studies statistically to estimate an overall effect.
Finding the gap between what people do and what they should do, and its cause.
A mistaken belief about the brain and learning. Many began as a real finding that was stretched or misread.
A statement of what someone will be able to do, written so it can be observed.
A shared belief that the group is safe for interpersonal risks, such as asking a question or admitting a mistake.
Whether an assessment gives the same result across assessors and occasions.
Recalling something from memory, which strengthens it.
Written criteria for judging a performance.
Support given to a learner and removed as they improve.
The agreement about what a piece of work includes and leaves out.
Spreading practice over time.
The person in the client organisation who wants the result and backs the work.
Using at work what was learned in training.
Whether an assessment measures what it claims to.
A problem shown with its full solution, for study.
Where people hold and work on information while they think. It is small.
